title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: On the eighth of September an officer came into the coach house where the prisoners were held. Judging by the respect the guards showed him, he was a very important one, probably someone on the staff. He held a paper in his hand and called over all the Russians there, naming Pierre as "the man who does not give his name." He glanced lazily and indifferently at all the prisoners, then ordered the officer in charge to have them decently dressed and tidied before taking them to the marshal. An hour later a squad of soldiers arrived, and Pierre and thirteen others were led to the Virgin's Field. It was a fine day, sunny after rain, and the air was unusually clear. The smoke didn't hang low, as on the day Pierre had been taken from the guardhouse on the Zubovski rampart, but rose through the clear air in columns. No flames were visible, but columns of smoke rose on every side, and all Moscow, as far as Pierre could see, was one vast charred ruin. Everywhere there were empty spaces with only stoves and chimney stacks left standing, and here and there the blackened walls of some brick houses. Pierre gazed at the ruins and did not recognize districts he had known well. Here and there he could see churches that hadn't burned. The Kremlin, which was not destroyed, gleamed white in the distance with its towers and the belfry of Ivan the Great. The domes of the New Convent of the Virgin glittered brightly and its bells were ringing particularly clearly. These bells reminded Pierre that it was Sunday and the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin. But there seemed to be no one to celebrate the holiday. Everywhere were blackened ruins, and the few Russians to be seen were tattered, frightened people who tried to hide when they saw the French.

The Russian nest was plainly ruined and destroyed. But Pierre sensed without quite knowing it that over this ruined nest a quite different, firm, French order had been set up in place of the Russian way of life. He felt it in the looks of the soldiers who were escorting him and the other criminals, marching in regular ranks, brisk and cheerful. He felt it in the look of an important French official in a carriage and pair, driven by a soldier, whom they met on the way. He felt it in the merry sounds of regimental music from the left side of the field, and he felt and understood it especially from the list of prisoners the French officer had read out that morning. One set of soldiers had taken Pierre and led him first to one place and then to another with dozens of other men, and it seemed they might have forgotten him or mixed him up with the others. But no: the answers he had given when questioned had come back to him in the label "the man who does not give his name." Under that name, which seemed terrible to Pierre, they were now leading him somewhere, with the unhesitating assurance on their faces that he and all the other prisoners were exactly the ones they wanted and were being taken to the right place. Pierre felt like an insignificant chip fallen among the wheels of a machine whose workings he didn't understand but which was running well.

He and the other prisoners were taken to the right side of the Virgin's Field, to a large white house with an immense garden, not far from the convent. This was Prince Shcherbatov's house, where Pierre had often been in other days. From the soldiers' talk he learned that the marshal, the Duke of Eckmühl (Davout), now occupied it.

They were taken to the entrance and led into the house one at a time. Pierre was the sixth to go in. He was taken through a glass gallery, an anteroom and a hall, all familiar to him, into a long low study, with an adjutant standing at the door.

Davout sat bent over a table at the far end of the room, with spectacles on his nose. Pierre went right up to him, but Davout, evidently reading a paper in front of him, did not look up. Without raising his eyes, he said in a low voice:
"Who are you?"

Pierre was silent because he couldn't utter a word. To him Davout was not merely a French general but a man notorious for his cruelty. He looked at that cold face, at the man sitting like a stern schoolmaster ready to wait a while for an answer, and felt that every moment's delay might cost him his life. But he didn't know what to say. He didn't dare repeat what he had said at his first examination, yet revealing his rank and position was dangerous and embarrassing. So he stayed silent. But before he had decided what to do, Davout raised his head, pushed his spectacles back onto his forehead, screwed up his eyes and looked at him intently.
"I know that man," he said in a cold, measured tone, evidently meant to frighten Pierre.
The chill that had been running down Pierre's back now gripped his head like a vise.
"You can't know me, General, I have never seen you..."
"He is a Russian spy," Davout interrupted, speaking to another general who was in the room, though Pierre hadn't noticed him.
Davout turned away. With an unexpected ring in his voice, Pierre began quickly:
"No, monseigneur," he said, suddenly remembering that Davout was a duke. "No, monseigneur, you can't have known me. I'm a militia officer and I haven't left Moscow."
"Your name?" asked Davout.
"Bezukhov."
"What proof have I that you are not lying?"
"Monseigneur!" exclaimed Pierre, not offended but pleading.

Davout looked up and gazed at him intently. For a few seconds they looked at each other, and that look saved Pierre. Quite apart from the conditions of war and law, that look set up a human relationship between the two men. In that moment a vast number of things passed dimly through both their minds, and they realized that they were both children of humanity and were brothers.

At the first glance, when Davout had only raised his head from the papers where human affairs and lives were shown as numbers, Pierre was merely a circumstance, and Davout could have shot him without burdening his conscience with an evil deed. But now he saw a human being in him. He thought for a moment.
"How can you show me that you are telling the truth?" said Davout coldly.
Pierre remembered Ramballe, and named him, his regiment and the street where the house was.
"You are not what you say," Davout answered.
In a trembling, faltering voice Pierre began to offer proofs that his statements were true.
But at that moment an adjutant came in and reported something to Davout.
Davout brightened at the news the adjutant brought and began buttoning up his uniform. He seemed to have forgotten Pierre completely.

When the adjutant reminded him of the prisoner, he jerked his head toward Pierre with a frown and ordered him taken away. But where they were to take him Pierre didn't know: back to the coach house, or to the place of execution his companions had pointed out as they crossed the Virgin's Field.
He turned his head and saw the adjutant putting another question to Davout.
"Yes, of course!" replied Davout, but what this "yes" meant, Pierre didn't know.

Pierre couldn't remember afterward how he walked, whether it was far, or in which direction. His faculties were numbed, he was stupefied, and he noticed nothing around him. He kept moving his legs as the others did until they all stopped and he stopped too. The only thought in his mind at that time was: who was it that had really sentenced him to death? Not the men on the commission that had first examined him: not one of them wished to do it or, evidently, could have. It wasn't Davout, who had looked at him in so human a way. In another moment Davout would have realized he was doing wrong, but just then the adjutant had come in and interrupted him. The adjutant, too, evidently had no evil intent, though he might have stayed out. Then who was executing him, killing him, taking his life, him, Pierre, with all his memories, aspirations, hopes and thoughts? Who was doing this? And Pierre felt that it was no one.
It was a system, a coming together of circumstances.
A system of some sort was killing him, Pierre, taking his life and everything else, wiping him out.
